title: A Randomised Trial of Combined Exercise Training Versus Waiting-List Control in Older Adults
abstract: Objective: To evaluate a combined aerobic and strength training programme delivered in community gyms as a treatment for depressive symptoms in older adults aged 60 years and over with major depressive disorder (DSM-5 criteria). Methods: In this randomised controlled trial, 82 older adults aged 60 years and over with major depressive disorder (DSM-5 criteria) were allocated at random to a combined aerobic and strength training programme delivered in community gyms or a waiting-list control. Participants were recruited from a mental health service in Australia. The primary outcome was change in the Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS). Results: Of 82 participants, 89% completed the 12-week assessment. Scores on the MADRS fell by 5.9 points in the exercise group and 2.1 points in the comparison group (between-group difference -3.8, 95% CI -5.6 to -2.2). Attendance at sessions averaged 70%. Conclusions: Structured exercise was associated with reduced depressive symptoms.

title: Exercise for Depression in Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials
abstract: Objective: To synthesise randomised controlled trials of exercise for women aged 20–45 years with depression. Methods: We searched five databases and included 45 trials (4106 participants). Results: Exercise reduced depressive symptoms compared with control conditions (standardised mean difference −0.60, 95% CI −0.92 to −0.25; I² = 52%). Conclusions: Exercise is an effective treatment for depression, although trial quality was variable.

title: Treadmill Exercise for Generalised Anxiety Disorder in Older Adults: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To assess supervised treadmill exercise at moderate intensity for 12 weeks in older adults aged 60 years and over with generalised anxiety disorder. Methods: 191 participants from urban primary care clinics in the United States were randomly assigned to exercise or health education sessions. The primary outcome was GAD-7 score. Results: GAD-7 score improved more in the exercise group (difference 1.7; p = 0.003). Conclusions: Exercise is a useful adjunct in generalised anxiety disorder care.

title: Sertraline for Late-Life Depression in Older Adults: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To test sertraline 50–200 mg daily for older adults aged 60 years and over with late-life depression (GDS-15 score of 6 or more). Methods: 131 participants from three university hospitals in Germany were randomly assigned to sertraline 50–200 mg daily or usual care. title: Group Walking for Heart Failure in Adult Outpatients: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To assess a group-based walking programme of 16 weeks in adult outpatients aged 18–70 years with chronic heart failure. Methods: 42 participants from outpatient psychiatric clinics in Sweden were randomly assigned to exercise or usual care. The primary outcome was peak oxygen uptake. Results: Peak oxygen uptake improved more in the exercise group (difference 1.5; p = 0.003). Conclusions: Exercise is a useful adjunct in heart failure care.

title: Acupuncture for Depressive Symptoms in Men: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To test acupuncture twice weekly for men aged 25–60 years with clinically significant depressive symptoms (PHQ-9 score of 10 or more). Methods: 242 participants from general practices in the United Kingdom were randomly assigned to acupuncture twice weekly or antidepressant medication alone. Conclusions: Acupuncture is a promising treatment for depression.

title: Treadmill Exercise for Mood in Older Adults Without Depression: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To test whether supervised treadmill exercise at moderate intensity for 12 weeks prevents the onset of depressive symptoms in older adults aged 60 years and over who were healthy volunteers with no history of depression. Methods: We randomised 201 older adults aged 60 years and over who were healthy volunteers with no history of depression (1:1) to supervised treadmill exercise at moderate intensity for 12 weeks or stretching and relaxation sessions, stratified by site. abstract: Background: Exercise may reduce depressive symptoms. Participants were recruited from primary care practices in the Netherlands; the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) was completed at baseline and follow-up. Results: Mean CES-D scores fell by 3.3 points (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Exercise appears feasible and acceptable in this group.

title: Physical Exercise in the Treatment of Depression in Community-Dwelling Adults: A Narrative Review
abstract: This review summarises evidence on resistance exercise for depression in community-dwelling adults aged 40–75 years, discusses proposed biological mechanisms, and outlines practical recommendations for general practitioners prescribing exercise.

title: Evaluation of Aerobic Exercise Versus Health Education Sessions in University Students

title: Prevalence and Correlates of COPD Among School Pupils: A Cross-Sectional Survey
abstract: Objective: To estimate the prevalence of copd among secondary school pupils aged 14–16 years. Methods: A cross-sectional survey of 2180 respondents from community health centres in Brazil. abstract: This review summarises evidence on resistance exercise for depression in adults aged 18 to 65 years, discusses proposed psychological mechanisms, and outlines practical recommendations for psychiatrists prescribing exercise.

title: Combined Exercise Training for Depression in Adults: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To evaluate a combined aerobic and strength training programme delivered in community gyms as a treatment for depressive symptoms in adults aged 18 to 65 years diagnosed with depression by their general practitioner. Results: Of 155 participants, 80% completed the 12-week assessment. Scores on the PHQ-9 fell by 9.0 points in the exercise group and 2.4 points in the comparison group (between-group difference -6.6, 95% CI -9.0 to -4.6). Adverse events were minor and mostly musculoskeletal. Conclusions: The findings support exercise as a treatment option in routine care.

title: Effects of Resistance Training on Depressive Symptoms in University Students
abstract: Objective: To evaluate progressive resistance training twice weekly for 10 weeks as a treatment for depressive symptoms in university students aged 18–30 years diagnosed with depression by their general practitioner. Adverse events were minor and mostly musculoskeletal. Conclusions: Benefits were modest; longer follow-up is needed.

title: Effects of High-Intensity Interval Training on Depressive Symptoms in School Pupils
abstract: Objective: To evaluate high-intensity interval training on a cycle ergometer, three times weekly for 8 weeks as a treatment for depressive symptoms in secondary school pupils aged 14–16 years with mild to moderate depression (BDI-II score of 14 or more). Methods: We randomised 111 secondary school pupils aged 14–16 years with mild to moderate depression (BDI-II score of 14 or more) (1:1) to high-intensity interval training on a cycle ergometer, three times weekly for 8 weeks or stretching and relaxation sessions, stratified by site. title: Bright Light Therapy for Mild to Moderate Depression in Community-Dwelling Adults: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To test bright light therapy each morning for community-dwelling adults aged 40–75 years with mild to moderate depression (BDI-II score of 14 or more). title: Aerobic Exercise for Type 2 Diabetes in Adult Outpatients: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To assess a 12-week supervised aerobic exercise programme (three 45-minute sessions per week) in adult outpatients aged 18–70 years with type 2 diabetes. Methods: 203 participants from community centres in South Korea were randomly assigned to exercise or stretching and relaxation sessions. The primary outcome was HbA1c. Results: HbA1c improved more in the exercise group (difference 7.8; p < 0.001). Conclusions: Exercise is a useful adjunct in type 2 diabetes care.

title: Aerobic Exercise for Obesity in Older Adults: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To assess a 12-week supervised aerobic exercise programme (three 45-minute sessions per week) in older adults aged 60 years and over with obesity. Methods: 60 participants from three university hospitals in Germany were randomly assigned to exercise or stretching and relaxation sessions. The primary outcome was body weight. Results: Body weight improved more in the exercise group (difference 11.3; p = 0.02). Conclusions: Exercise is a useful adjunct in obesity care.

title: Group Walking for Knee Osteoarthritis in University Students: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To assess a group-based walking programme of 16 weeks in university students aged 18–30 years with knee osteoarthritis. Methods: 227 participants from urban primary care clinics in the United States were randomly assigned to exercise or stretching and relaxation sessions. The primary outcome was WOMAC function score. Results: WOMAC function score improved more in the exercise group (difference 1.6; p < 0.001). Conclusions: Exercise is a useful adjunct in knee osteoarthritis care.

title: Feasibility of High-Intensity Interval Training for Mild to Moderate Depression: A Single-Arm Pilot Study
abstract: Background: Exercise may reduce depressive symptoms. Methods: In this single-arm pilot study, all 254 university students aged 18–30 years with mild to moderate depression (BDI-II score of 14 or more) received high-intensity interval training on a cycle ergometer, three times weekly for 8 weeks; there was no control group. Participants were recruited from a mental health service in Australia; the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II) was completed at baseline and follow-up. Results: Mean BDI-II scores fell by 4.2 points (p = 0.01). Conclusions: A randomised trial is warranted.

title: High-Intensity Interval Training for Chronic Low Back Pain in Adults: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To assess high-intensity interval training on a cycle ergometer, three times weekly for 8 weeks in adults aged 18 to 65 years with chronic low back pain. title: A Randomised Trial of Group Walking Versus Waiting-List Control in Young People

title: Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for Major Depressive Disorder in Community-Dwelling Adults: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To test an 8-week mindfulness-based cognitive therapy course for community-dwelling adults aged 40–75 years with major depressive disorder (DSM-5 criteria). title: Behavioural Activation for Treatment-Resistant Depression in University Students: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To test behavioural activation delivered by lay counsellors for university students aged 18–30 years with treatment-resistant depression. Methods: 199 participants from primary care practices in the Netherlands were randomly assigned to behavioural activation delivered by lay counsellors or health education sessions. title: Treadmill Exercise and Recovery from Mild to Moderate Depression: A Prospective Cohort Study
abstract: Background: Exercise may reduce depressive symptoms. Participants were recruited from rehabilitation centres in Spain; the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D) was completed at baseline and follow-up. Results: Mean CES-D scores fell by 8.2 points (p = 0.04). Conclusions: A randomised trial is warranted.

title: Resistance Training for Hypertension in Adult Outpatients: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To assess progressive resistance training twice weekly for 10 weeks in adult outpatients aged 18–70 years with stage 1 hypertension. Methods: 236 participants from general practices in the United Kingdom were randomly assigned to exercise or health education sessions. The primary outcome was 24-hour systolic blood pressure. Results: 24-hour systolic blood pressure improved more in the exercise group (difference 3.0; p = 0.02). Conclusions: Exercise is a useful adjunct in hypertension care.

title: Aerobic Exercise for Cancer-Related Fatigue in Adults: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To assess a 12-week supervised aerobic exercise programme (three 45-minute sessions per week) in adults aged 18 to 65 years with cancer-related fatigue after breast cancer treatment. title: Resistance Training for Obesity in Adults: A Randomised Controlled Trial
abstract: Objective: To assess progressive resistance training twice weekly for 10 weeks in adults aged 18 to 65 years with obesity. title: Prevalence and Correlates of Chronic Low Back Pain Among Adolescents: A Cross-Sectional Survey
abstract: Objective: To estimate the prevalence of chronic low back pain among adolescents aged 13–17 years. Methods: A cross-sectional survey of 2780 respondents from a mental health service in Australia. Results: Prevalence was 10.8%, and was higher among those with lower income. Conclusions: Targeted screening is recommended.

title: Prevalence and Correlates of Heart Failure Among Adults: A Cross-Sectional Survey
abstract: Objective: To estimate the prevalence of heart failure among adults aged 18 to 65 years. Methods: A cross-sectional survey of 1520 respondents from a mental health service in Australia. Results: Prevalence was 14.7%, and was higher among those with lower income. Conclusions: Targeted screening is recommended.

title: A Randomised Trial of Group Walking Versus Usual Care in Children
abstract: Objective: To evaluate a group-based walking programme of 16 weeks as a treatment for depressive symptoms in children aged 8–12 years diagnosed with depression by their general practitioner.
